section_summary: This section documents Allied disagreement over Japanese Antarctic whaling, including Australian objections to Japanese crews and flags, U.S. and SCAP replies, and inspection and conservation questions. It also contains Japanese coastal catch reports, Antarctic fleet status tables, whale catcher and shore station inventories, and whaling regulations. Later pages address American access to Japanese agar weed and a Japanese request to resume fishing in northern Pacific waters.

subfiles.title: U.S. aide-mémoire on Australian proposals for Allied whaling crews
subfiles.about: The United States declines Australia's proposal to crew the Antarctic whaling expedition entirely with Allied nationals.
subfiles.summary: SCAP regards converting vessels and managing mixed Allied crews as impractical, but welcomes additional Allied inspectors. The aide-mémoire describes the expedition as a one-season emergency operation under SCAP control, addresses its flag, and reserves future Japanese whaling rights for Allied decision.

subfiles.title: Correction of Antarctic whaling flag description
subfiles.about: The Department corrects its description of the expedition's flag.
subfiles.summary: The flag will use modified code flag E rather than O.

subfiles.title: Australian protest against display of Japanese merchant marine flag
subfiles.about: Australia asks that SCAP's November 15 whaling flag directive be rescinded.
subfiles.summary: Australia says display of the Japanese merchant marine flag contradicts U.S. assurances and could imply that the expedition is Japanese.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Major Plimsoll on whaling flags
subfiles.about: Major Plimsoll delivers Australia's flag protest and explains its political significance.
subfiles.summary: Penfield promises inquiries and a prompt reply.

subfiles.title: U.S. reply on the Antarctic whaling flag
subfiles.about: The United States reports SCAP's decision to remove the Japanese merchant marine flag from expedition vessels.
subfiles.summary: After international notice, the vessels will fly only the modified international E flag; Navy and SCAP have been informed.

subfiles.title: Australian statement opposing renewed Japanese Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Australia urges prohibition of another Japanese Antarctic expedition and offers Allied operation of whaling ships.
subfiles.summary: The speaker cites security risks, past conservation violations, wasteful processing, and the international catch limit. He recounts Australian protests and U.S. assurances, then criticizes the authorization of a second Japanese expedition without meaningful Allied consultation. Australia offers to crew and operate ships, supply food and oil for Japan, and work with other Allied governments; the statement moves adoption of FEC-231/4.

subfiles.title: Department inquiry to SCAP on Allied whaling crews
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department requests SCAP's comments on Australia's renewed proposal to use Allied crews.
subfiles.summary: The Department considers the proposal impractical and also requests answers about whaling inspection.

subfiles.title: Draft continuation of Allied crews telegram
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: A marked draft repeats the Department's request for SCAP's views on Allied crews.
subfiles.summary: Draft continuation of the October 7 telegram, marked not sent.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply on feasibility of Allied whaling crews
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: SCAP rejects mixed Allied crews as impractical for the imminent whaling expedition.
subfiles.summary: Vessel conversion, delay, divided authority, conflicting laws, and crew support would obstruct the expedition.

subfiles.title: SCAP report on whaling inspectors, penalties, biology and right whale
subfiles.about: Tokyo answers Department questions about whaling oversight and a reported right whale catch.
subfiles.summary: The telegram describes Japanese inspector qualifications and penalties, planned biological investigations, and records showing no right whales taken during Bonin operations. It asks for evidence behind the contrary report.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into reported 1945 right whale catch
subfiles.about: The Department requests urgent explanation of a Japanese report indicating one right whale was taken.
subfiles.summary: A report obtained through Dr. Remington Kellogg is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Department questions on whaling oversight and tanker conversion
subfiles.about: The Department seeks information for the whaling conference and comments on tanker conversions.
subfiles.summary: It asks about American inspectors and the Antarctic project file, and notes British and New Zealand objections to converting three tankers.

subfiles.title: Despatch 646 forwarding Japanese whaling reports
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwards coastal catch, Antarctic fleet, and whale catcher reports.
subfiles.summary: Reports cover September 8–14 and list Japanese whale catcher boats.

subfiles.title: Japanese coastal whaling report, September 8–14
subfiles.from: Japanese Bureau of Fisheries via SCAP
subfiles.about: The report lists operating shore stations, catchers and species counts for a week of coastal whaling.
subfiles.summary: It records 102 whales, predominantly sperm whales.

subfiles.title: Antarctic whaling fleet status, September 8–14
subfiles.doc_type: fleet status report with duplicate sheets
subfiles.from: Japanese Bureau of Fisheries via SCAP
subfiles.about: The tables track construction, conversion and operation of vessels intended for the 1946–47 Antarctic fleet.
subfiles.summary: Factory ships, carriers, a tanker and catchers are listed by tonnage, location, work and estimated completion. Pages 498–500 repeat clearer versions of entries on pages 495–497.

subfiles.title: Inventory of Japanese whale catcher boats
subfiles.about: The inventory identifies Japanese whale catcher boats, their owners, tonnage, power and construction.
subfiles.summary: It counts 36 existing and eight boats under construction, noting Antarctic authorization.

subfiles.title: Duplicate inventory of Japanese whale catcher boats
subfiles.about: A second copy repeats the whale catcher inventory.
subfiles.summary: Lists 44 existing or planned catcher boats.

subfiles.title: Despatch 647 forwarding weekly whaling reports
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwards weekly catches, fleet status, a shore station list and map.
subfiles.summary: Enclosures concern September 15–21 whaling activities and Japanese shore stations.

subfiles.title: Japanese coastal whaling report, September 15–21
subfiles.from: Japanese Bureau of Fisheries via SCAP
subfiles.about: The report lists coastal station catches and inactive whale catcher boats.
subfiles.summary: It records 54 whales and explains vessels idle for transit, repairs or salvage.

subfiles.title: Antarctic whaling fleet status, September 15–21
subfiles.doc_type: fleet status report with duplicate sheets
subfiles.from: Japanese Bureau of Fisheries via SCAP
subfiles.about: The tables update conversion and readiness of the 1946–47 Antarctic fleet.
subfiles.summary: The report tracks factory ships, carriers, tanker and catcher construction and repairs, including a catcher removed after beaching at Ayukawa. Pages 511–516 contain repeated copies of entries on pages 508–510.

subfiles.title: List of Japanese whaling land stations
subfiles.about: The list locates whaling stations and identifies their operating companies.
subfiles.summary: Twenty-three locations contain 29 company stations.

subfiles.title: Map of Japanese whaling land stations
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: A two-page map plots Japanese whaling shore stations by company.
subfiles.summary: Map accompanying despatch 647.

subfiles.title: Despatch 649 forwarding whaling laws and inspection memorandum
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwards Japanese whaling regulations, penalty provisions and a SCAP memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Four enclosures address inspectors and whaling violations.

subfiles.title: Regulation Law of Factory Whaling
subfiles.about: The extract sets limits on factory whaling, protected whales, seasons, processing and crew remuneration.
subfiles.summary: It prohibits taking right and gray whales, calves and undersized whales, and requires fuller use of catches.

subfiles.title: Ministerial ordinance changing the 1946–47 whaling season
subfiles.from: Hiroo Wada, Minister of Agriculture and Forestry
subfiles.about: The ordinance permits baleen whaling south of 40°S for a specified season but excludes humpbacks.
subfiles.summary: Baleen season: December 6 to April 7; humpback catch prohibited.

subfiles.title: Fisheries Law penalty provisions
subfiles.about: Extracts describe licensing requirements, fines, confiscation and penalties for fisheries violations.
subfiles.summary: Factory fishing and whaling require permission; violations can incur fines or forfeiture.

subfiles.title: SCAP memorandum on whaling inspection and enforcement
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains inspector qualifications, legal penalties, biological studies and reported right whale catches.
subfiles.summary: It describes two inspectors per factory ship, identifies penalties under Japanese law and SCAP directives, and says stronger rules are being prepared. Biological instructions await Washington guidance; SCAP records show no right whale caught in the Bonins.

subfiles.title: Charles E. Jackson letter introducing agar correspondence
subfiles.about: Jackson forwards correspondence on American agar production and Shipman's proposed trip to Japan.
subfiles.summary: He notes Chairman Bland's interest and may follow up.

subfiles.title: Shipman letter to Bland about agar appeal
subfiles.about: Shipman sends Bland a draft appeal to the Secretary of War for help with agar supplies.
subfiles.summary: He requests Bland's advice and support.

subfiles.title: American Agar and Chemical Company appeal for Japanese Gelidium
subfiles.about: Shipman seeks Japanese Gelidium supplies and permission to visit Japan to arrange procurement.
subfiles.summary: He explains agar's laboratory importance, prewar reliance on Japan, and the company's limited Mexican and Californian supplies. Purchasing Japanese weed, he argues, would sustain U.S. production while providing Japan dollar income. He requests a short visit to work out arrangements.

subfiles.title: Bland letter supporting American agar production
subfiles.about: Bland urges federal study of obtaining Japanese Gelidium for American agar manufacture.
subfiles.summary: He stresses agar's essential uses and the company's wartime role, and asks for coordinated consideration by federal departments.

subfiles.title: Flory reply to Carver on whaling conservation
subfiles.about: Flory discusses the Antarctic catch limit, Japanese whaling safeguards and a draft conference proposal.
subfiles.summary: He favors retaining a catch limit while recognizing that 16,000 blue whale units may exceed a conservation target. He summarizes assurances on the one-season Japanese expedition and invites Carver's comments before the whaling conference.

subfiles.title: Despatch 657 on Japanese request to fish northern waters
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwards Japan's request to resume fishing around Kamchatka and the Kurils and asks for U.S. views.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser notes Japanese food needs and earlier Soviet fishing arrangements, but expects strong U.S. opposition to operations near the Bering Sea and Aleutians.

subfiles.title: Japanese request for permission to fish in northern waters
subfiles.about: Japan requests expansion of its authorized fishing area around Kamchatka, the Bering Sea and Kurils.
subfiles.summary: The request cites experienced fishermen and food shortages.

subfiles.title: Fishery in the Northern Waters
subfiles.about: Japan proposes 1947 crab, salmon, trawling and whaling operations in northern waters.
subfiles.summary: The proposal cites prewar production and protein shortages, then outlines fleets and projected catches. Its detailed plan continues beyond page 539.
